prompt: As countries try to reduce their carbon emissions, some argue that nuclear power must be part of the solution, while others believe that only renewable sources such as wind and solar should be developed. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
essay:
Reducing emissions quickly enough to meet climate targets requires decisions about which low-carbon technologies to build. Some argue that nuclear generation is indispensable; others maintain that wind and solar can do the whole job. I believe nuclear power has to be included, mainly because of what happens when the weather does not cooperate.

The case against nuclear energy is not irrational. Construction costs have consistently exceeded forecasts, and plants take well over a decade to complete, which is a serious objection when the emissions problem is urgent. The waste question also remains genuinely unresolved in most countries, and although the risk of a major accident is very low, the consequences when one occurs are unusually long-lasting and fall on people who did not choose them.

The difficulty for a renewables-only strategy is reliability. Wind and solar output varies by hour and by season, and a grid must match supply to demand continuously. Storage at the scale required to cover several still, dark winter days does not yet exist at acceptable cost. Without a controllable low-carbon source, the gap tends to be filled by gas, which means a renewables-only policy can in practice mean a renewables-plus-fossil-fuel policy. The same objection applies to interconnection between countries, which only helps if a neighbour happens to have surplus power at the exact hour of the shortfall; large weather systems frequently sit over several neighbouring countries at once.

My own view is that this last point is decisive. The realistic comparison is not nuclear against renewables but nuclear against the gas plants that would otherwise cover the shortfall. Judged that way, extending the life of existing reactors and building a limited number of new ones is the lower risk, even accounting for cost overruns and the unsolved problem of long-term storage.
title: Nuclear power in a low-carbon energy mix
